status_summary: The administration moved to end Flores through the courts: the Justice Department moved to terminate the settlement on 2025-05-22, Chief Judge Dolly M. Gee denied the motion on 2025-08-15, and the government appealed; the Ninth Circuit heard argument on 2026-06-02 (No. 25-6308) and no decision was found. On 2026-08-17 the district court appointed a Special Master and Independent Monitor to oversee compliance with the settlement at CBP border sectors, the Dilley facility and hotels used to house children. No statute repealing or amending TVPRA section 235, setting national detention standards or moving custody of unaccompanied children from HHS to DHS was found, and the Office of Refugee Resettlement still runs the program. HHS proposed a rule on 2026-06-26 that would tighten sponsor identity, income and background checks for released children, with comments due 2026-08-25.

timeline.event: The government filed a motion in the Central District of California (Flores v. Bondi, Doc. 1567) to terminate the Flores Settlement Agreement under its paragraph 40 and Rule 60(b)(4), (5) and (6) and to dissolve the court's injunction of the 2019 DHS regulations; CBS News reported the filing the same day.
timeline.source: C.D. Cal. motion (Doc. 1567; copy posted by National Center for Youth Law)

timeline.event: Chief Judge Dolly M. Gee denied the government's motion to terminate the Flores Settlement Agreement and dissolve the 2019 injunction (Flores v. Bondi, No. CV 85-4544-DMG), finding no basis for relief under Rule 60(b) and holding that termination requires final federal regulations implementing the agreement, with termination to occur 45 days after such regulations are published.
The Ninth Circuit heard argument at Seattle on 2026-06-02 in the government's appeal of the denial (Flores v. Blanche, No. 25-6308), as listed on the court's monthly sittings calendar.

HHS's Administration for Children and Families (Office of Refugee Resettlement) proposed a rule requiring specified identity documents, proof of income and wider background checks for sponsors of unaccompanied children and aligning background-check rules with the 2025 reconciliation act (comments to 2026-08-25); no effective date was set.

In Flores v. Blanche (C.D. Cal., No. CV 85-4544-DMG) Chief Judge Dolly M. Gee discharges the court's 2026-06-15 order to show cause (Doc. 1794) and, by Docs. 1827 and 1828, appoints a Special Master and Independent Monitor to monitor compliance with the Flores Settlement Agreement for an initial 12 months, covering time in custody and conditions in the CBP Rio Grande Valley, El Paso and San Diego sectors, the Dilley facility and hotels used to house class members; the settlement remains in force and enforced while the government's appeal of the termination denial is pending.
timeline.source: C.D. Cal. orders (Docs. 1827 and 1828; copy posted by National Center for Youth Law)

title: Repeal TVPRA section 235, end the Flores agreement, move child custody from HHS to DHS
uncertainties: The filing date of the motion (2025-05-22, Doc. 1567) comes from a copy of the motion posted by plaintiffs' counsel and a CBS News report of the same date, and was not checked against the docket; the motion noticed a hearing for 2025-07-18, so the hearing was apparently reset; the order read (Doc. 1637, 2025-08-15, on a copy posted by plaintiffs' counsel) gives only its hearing date of 2025-08-08 and denies the motion under Rule 60(b). The Ninth Circuit argument is listed on the court's monthly sittings calendar (which notes entries may change before the hearing; the page is not itself marked provisional) and reported by Bloomberg Government, which says the panel questioned the case for ending the decree; plaintiffs' counsel's case page lists briefing from December 2025 to February 2026 and no decision, and searches found none. The calendar page could not be re-fetched in the 2026-10-22 pass, so the argument and the absence of a decision were not re-verified then. The district court's order says the agreement ends 45 days after final implementing regulations are published, so a final DHS or HHS Flores rule, none of which was found, is the route the court named. The orders appointing a Special Master and Independent Monitor (Docs. 1827 and 1828) are dated and filed 2026-08-17, not 2026-08-18 as an advocacy case page gave; they were opened on copies posted by plaintiffs' counsel (the National Center for Youth Law and the Center for Human Rights and Constitutional Law), which agree. A mirror of the 2025 order on a rejected wrapper host was not used. Bills introduced in December 2025 (H.R. 6389 and S. 3322) would loosen fees and information sharing for unaccompanied children in the opposite direction and neither addresses TVPRA, Flores or custody. No administration bill on this topic and no DHS rule on alien minors was found in a Federal Register search. HHS sponsor-rule changes are a related ORR vetting step, not custody transfer. Litigation over Flores as a DOJ priority is also covered in c17-06.
